Tópicos A • Lecture 15

Segmentation & Detection

Thiago Medeiros

Task taxonomy, metrics, and a practical demo with pretrained models

Goals for today

  • Understand what changes when we move from classification to dense prediction.
  • Be fluent with the main metrics: IoU, mAP, mIoU, Dice.
  • Know the core building blocks: backbone, FPN, heads, NMS.
  • Run a pretrained detector/segmenter in PyTorch and interpret its failure modes.

Format Semi-lab: short theory + hands-on inference + error analysis.

1. Task taxonomy (Vision)

From global to dense

  • Classification: one label per image
  • Localization: one box + one label
  • Detection: many boxes + many labels
  • Segmentation: label per pixel (and maybe per instance)

Same backbone family, but different outputs, losses, and evaluation.

Exemplo real (foto) com sobreposições. Foto: Papito/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.5 / CC BY-SA 3.0).

Segmentation flavors

  • Semantic: each pixel → class
  • Instance: separate masks per object
  • Panoptic: semantic + instance together

Rule of thumb: if you care about counting and per-object properties, you likely need instance/panoptic.

Mesmo exemplo real, com diferentes espaços de rótulos. Foto: Papito/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.5 / CC BY-SA 3.0).

2. Object detection: the pipeline

Core components

  • Backbone (CNN): feature extraction
  • Neck (often FPN): multi-scale features
  • Head: classification + box regression
  • Post-processing: score threshold + NMS

Most modern detectors are variations on this theme.

Backbone → FPN → Head(s) → NMS → final boxes.

Two big families

Two-stage

  • Faster R-CNN: proposals (RPN) → refine + classify
  • Often higher accuracy, slower inference

Key idea explicitly propose candidate regions.

One-stage

  • RetinaNet, YOLO-style: dense predictions over a grid
  • Usually faster, competitive accuracy

Key idea no explicit proposal step.

3. IoU (Intersection over Union)

Detection & segmentation rely on overlap-based metrics.

Definition

$$\mathrm{IoU}(A,B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}$$

  • Used to match predicted boxes to ground-truth boxes
  • Used directly as segmentation score (pixel IoU)

Common thresholds 0.5, 0.75, and COCO-style averages.

Drag the boxes. Watch IoU update live.

mAP (mean Average Precision)

  • For each class: build a precision–recall curve
  • AP = area under that curve
  • mAP = mean AP over classes

COCO reports AP averaged over multiple IoU thresholds (0.50:0.95).

Toy PR curve (qualitative). Higher is better.

Why NMS exists

Dense models often predict many overlapping boxes for the same object.

Greedy NMS (typical)

  1. Keep the highest-score box
  2. Suppress boxes with IoU > threshold
  3. Repeat with remaining boxes

Trade-off Too low → misses nearby objects. Too high → duplicates.

Kept: —
Suppressed boxes are faded.

Segmentation metrics

mIoU (mean IoU)

  • Compute IoU per class over pixels
  • Average over classes (careful with rare classes)

Dice / F1

$$\mathrm{Dice}(A,B) = \frac{2|A \cap B|}{|A| + |B|}$$

Often preferred for medical segmentation and highly imbalanced masks.

Same overlap, different scalings: Dice is more forgiving for small objects.

4. Demo: pretrained models in torchvision

We will use off-the-shelf models (COCO pretrained) to get intuition fast.

  • Detection: Faster R-CNN RetinaNet
  • Instance segmentation: Mask R-CNN
  • Semantic segmentation: FCN DeepLabV3

Reminder These models are trained on COCO: expect domain shift on your data.

Detection inference (Faster R-CNN)

import torch
from torchvision.models.detection import fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn, FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights
from torchvision.io import read_image

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

weights = FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights.DEFAULT
model = fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights=weights).to(device).eval()

img = read_image("my_image.jpg")  # uint8 [C,H,W]
preprocess = weights.transforms()
x = preprocess(img).to(device)    # float tensor, normalized

with torch.no_grad():
    out = model([x])[0]  # dict: boxes, labels, scores

# Filter by confidence
keep = out["scores"] > 0.50
boxes = out["boxes"][keep]
labels = out["labels"][keep]
scores = out["scores"][keep]

Key idea: the weights.transforms() gives the exact preprocessing expected by the pretrained weights.

Visualize boxes (torchvision utils)

from torchvision.utils import draw_bounding_boxes
from torchvision.transforms.functional import to_pil_image

class_names = weights.meta["categories"]

annotated = draw_bounding_boxes(
    img, boxes=boxes,
    labels=[f"{class_names[l]}:{s:.2f}" for l, s in zip(labels, scores)],
    width=3
)

to_pil_image(annotated).save("det_result.jpg")

For quick exploration, qualitative analysis is often enough to spot dataset shift.

Instance segmentation (Mask R-CNN)

from torchvision.models.detection import maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn, MaskRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights

w = MaskRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights.DEFAULT
m = maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights=w).to(device).eval()
x = w.transforms()(img).to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    out = m([x])[0]

# out["masks"] : [N, 1, H, W] with probabilities
keep = out["scores"] > 0.60
masks = out["masks"][keep] > 0.5
boxes = out["boxes"][keep]

Masks are probabilistic. You choose a binarization threshold (e.g., 0.5).

Semantic segmentation (DeepLabV3)

from torchvision.models.segmentation import deeplabv3_resnet50, DeepLabV3_ResNet50_Weights

w = DeepLabV3_ResNet50_Weights.DEFAULT
model = deeplabv3_resnet50(weights=w).to(device).eval()
x = w.transforms()(img).to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(x.unsqueeze(0))["out"][0]  # [C,H,W]
pred = logits.argmax(0).cpu()                 # [H,W] class indices

Semantic seg gives a class per pixel. No instance separation.

Common failure modes (use Lecture 14 mindset)

Detection

  • Missed small objects (scale)
  • Confusing visually similar classes
  • Duplicate boxes (NMS too high / borderline IoU)
  • Domain shift (lighting, camera, viewpoint)

Segmentation

  • Boundary errors (blurred edges)
  • Thin structures vanish
  • Class imbalance (rare class ignored)
  • Label ambiguity / noisy masks

Always ask: is it data, model capacity, or objective/metric mismatch?

5. Semi-lab (40–50 min)

Deliverable: short report (1 page) + a folder with visual outputs.

  1. Select 10 images (your dataset or any set with variety).
  2. Run Faster R-CNN (or RetinaNet) with 3 thresholds: 0.30 / 0.50 / 0.70.
  3. Run Mask R-CNN on the same images (threshold 0.60).
  4. For each image, annotate:
    • 2 good detections / segmentations
    • 2 failure cases (missed, wrong class, poor mask)
  5. Write 3 concrete hypotheses explaining the failures (dataset shift, small objects, occlusion, etc.).

Tip Keep everything in eval() + torch.no_grad() for speed.

Optional extension: quick imbalance hack

If you do fine-tuning later, you will face class imbalance. A quick baseline:

# For training loaders (classification / segmentation):
from torch.utils.data import WeightedRandomSampler

# weights[i] = inverse frequency of class for sample i (toy idea)
sampler = WeightedRandomSampler(weights, num_samples=len(weights), replacement=True)

loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=32, sampler=sampler)

This is simplistic (especially for detection/segmentation), but it often improves early training stability.

Checklist before leaving

  • Do you understand what IoU means and how it impacts AP/NMS?
  • Can you explain the difference between semantic and instance segmentation?
  • Do your qualitative errors suggest data issues or model issues?
